newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bundesbank officials warn of EMU delay past 1999.
newsitem.headline: Bundesbank officials warn of EMU delay past 1999.

text.p: The European Union must launch its planned single currency on time or risk serious set-backs even though Germany -- the driving force behind integration -- might itself miss key entry targets, senior German central bank officials said on Monday night.

Three members of the Bundesbank's ruling council, speaking at separate events in Germany, warned that nations struggling to meet the fiscal entry criteria while still recovering from severe recession should avoid any temptation to postpone the 1999 start of monetary union.

Although this might seem like a less painful and therefore desirable option, Guntram Palm, president of the state central bank in Baden Wuerttemberg, said all talk of delaying the start date was "totally misplaced".
Such a decision would lead to an immediate, severe appreciation of the mark, which would hurt German exports as well as stunt nations' efforts to achieve a further consolidation of finances.

One reason that talk of a delay has reached new heights might be that so many nations, including Germany, risked missing the key criteria which call for an aspiring nation's budget deficit to remain below three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) and that its debt should not exceed a reference value of 60 percent of GDP.

Klaus-Dieter Kuehbacher, president of the state central bank in Berlin and Brandenburg, said he doubted whether the German government would reach its goal of holding its budget deficit to 2.9 percent of GDP in 1997.
But the three also acknowledged that the deficit goal was only one of a number of entry critieria and that it might ultimately not be the most instrumental to sustaining a stable currency union.
The Maastricht Treaty also states that participating nations must present stable foreign exchange rates as well as low long-term interest and inflation rates and many more nations fulfil these goals.

"In my opinion European currency union can start in January 1999 while conforming to those EMU convergence criteria that are most often discussed," said Ernst Welteke, president of the state central bank in Hesse.
Welteke said he wondered how a budget deficit of just under three percent would be good for stability while a budget deficit of slightly over three percent would be negative.
At the same time he added: "Fiscal stability in currency union is naturally a very important asset as it ensures that fiscal solidity of the individual members can be closely monitored."

Fearing strict entry criteria could give way to creative book-keeping, Palm said "a trick-free deficit of just over three percent in 1997 that will be further reduced in following years due to savings efforts is preferable to 2.9 percent reached through creative accounting."
Welteke added that "the three percent deficit criteria should note be a knock-out criteria", prohibiting any nation just over that level from entering.
Both Palm and Welteke feel the currency union will go ahead as planned with Germany and France, noting a currency union without them would make little sense.

Officials however part ways on whether the union will be a small or a slightly larger one at the beginning. Palm, noting most nations already meet the other criteria, forecast a bigger circle but Kuehbacher saw fewer members.
"A start with a small circle therefore seems sensible," Kuehbacher said, adding however that the benefits, including an expected push in investment growth, would first be smaller.
But the benefits would grow as more EU members joined monetary union at a later date, Kuehbacher added.
